title: The eyes
hookLine: eyes half open, gaze resting on the floor ahead

lines: A CAT WITH EYES IN SLITS.
cards: A cat lies on a sunny windowsill, eyes narrowed to slits. Asleep? Drop a spoon in the kitchen and the ears turn instantly.
Not asleep. Not exactly watching, either. Resting, and still there.
Ask people what meditation looks like and they'll often shut their eyes to show you. Zen asks for something else: the eyes partly open, lids lowered, gaze on the floor ahead. A little like that cat.

teach.h: LIDS HALF DOWN, GAZE ON THE FLOOR.
teach.b: In zazen the eyes are neither shut nor wide. The lids come halfway down, and the gaze rests on the floor a little way ahead, or on the wall if you're facing one. It isn't fixed on a spot.
It's soft, the way eyes rest when someone is listening hard to music. Dogen's guide to sitting is plain about it: keep the eyes open.
Why not closed? Two things tend to happen. Drowsiness creeps in, the body taking the hint that it's bedtime.
Or a private movie starts: plans, memories, imaginary arguments, and the mind wanders off into its own theater. Half open keeps a little daylight in.
Why not wide? Wide eyes grab. They pick out a crack in the paint, a speck on the floor, the person shifting next to you, and attention follows each one.
Lowering the lids takes the grip out of looking. Things are still seen; they just aren't chased.

teach.h: HALF OPEN: IN THE ROOM, AT REST.
teach.b: Half open is the same pair as the rest of this week. Straight and relaxed in the back.
Thumbs just touching in the hands. Here, in the eyes: present to the room, not hunting through it. The world isn't shut out, and it isn't grabbed.
Half-open eyes keep the sitter in the room, at rest.

how: In Zen halls, people commonly sit with eyes half open and gaze lowered; in Soto Zen they often sit facing a wall, and in Rinzai Zen facing into the room.

o: eyes shut tight to keep the world out
lids half lowered, gaze resting softly ahead
eyes fixed hard on a single point

s: in zazen the eyes are always closed
Dogen's guide says to keep them open; in practice they're half open, gaze lowered.
the gaze in zazen is fixed hard on one spot
it rests softly, unfocused, on the floor ahead.
half-open eyes help keep drowsiness away

games.q: you're sitting zazen and your eyes keep sliding shut. you feel sleep coming. what do you do?
o: let them close; it's more peaceful
lift the lids a little and lower the gaze again
open them wide and stare at a spot
games.why: lift the lids back to half open. closed invites drowsiness; wide invites grabbing. half open is the middle.

practice: In your posture, hands resting, let the eyelids come halfway down and the gaze drop softly to the floor a little way ahead, not fixed on any spot.
If the eyes start to close, lift the lids a little; if they start to hunt around, let them settle back. Shapes and light can stay at the edges, and nothing needs looking at.

wordCard.voice: The eyes. In zazen, half open, lids lowered, the gaze resting softly on the floor ahead: neither shut out nor grabbing. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: half open. The room stays, and nothing in it needs chasing. See you on the cushion tomorrow.
